sourceScope: Fresh paraphrased StudyDock exam revision based on selected scanned pages 11–66 of TARGET HIGH BOOK 151-300.pdf (Part 2). NOT a full Part 2 extraction; textbook printed page numbers differ from PDF page indices.
rightsNotice: StudyDock-authored summaries and adapted MCQs. No verbatim original textbook questions, scanned textbook images, or copied diagrams are included in this public JSON.

levels.title: Digestive tract & organ functions
levels.summary: Learn digestive tract & organ functions through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Core concept
concepts.body: The gastrointestinal tract is a continuous pathway for food and digestive contents. The textbook illustration labels the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus. Associated digestive organs include the liver, gallbladder and pancreas.
concepts.example: Small intestine: duodenum → jejunum → ileum.

concepts.title: Mouth to stomach
concepts.body: Mechanical breakdown and swallowing begin at the mouth. The oesophagus conveys swallowed material into the stomach. Its upper and lower sphincters help coordinate passage of contents.
concepts.example: Liver and pancreas contribute digestive secretions, but food does not pass through these organs.

concepts.title: Intestinal organisation
concepts.body: The small intestine is divided into the duodenum, jejunum and ileum; digestion and nutrient absorption occur mainly here. The large intestine includes the caecum, colon, rectum and anal canal and is important for water and stool handling.
concepts.example: Large intestine includes ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid colon.

quiz.prompt: Which structure carries swallowed food from the pharynx toward the stomach?
quiz.explanation: The oesophagus is the muscular tube joining the pharynx to the stomach.

quiz.prompt: What is the correct order of the three portions of the small intestine?
quiz.explanation: The small intestine progresses from the duodenum to jejunum and then ileum.

quiz.prompt: Which is a major function of the small intestine?
quiz.explanation: Much digestion and absorption takes place in the small intestine.

quiz.prompt: Which structure is primarily responsible for bile storage?
quiz.explanation: The liver makes bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.

quiz.prompt: Which layer lines the inner surface of the gastrointestinal tract?
quiz.explanation: The mucosa is the innermost layer in contact with luminal contents.

levels.title: Digestion & GI procedures
levels.summary: Learn digestion & gi procedures through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Digestive process
concepts.body: Food must be broken into smaller components that can be absorbed. The source's digestion table distinguishes carbohydrate, protein and fat digestion along the digestive tract.
concepts.example: Villi and microvilli increase intestinal absorptive surface area.

concepts.title: Main locations
concepts.body: The mouth starts food processing and salivary activity. In the stomach, gastric secretions participate particularly in protein digestion. In the small intestine, pancreatic enzymes and bile act with the intestinal environment to enable digestion and absorption.
concepts.example: Pancreatic enzymes participate in protein, carbohydrate and fat digestion.

concepts.title: Layered wall
concepts.body: From inner to outer, the source describes a mucosal lining, submucosa, muscular layer and serosa/adventitia. Circular and longitudinal muscles support movement. The mucosa contacts luminal contents; the submucosa carries supporting structures.
concepts.example: The colon contributes to stool formation and water conservation.

quiz.prompt: Which pancreatic enzyme is most directly associated with fat digestion?
quiz.explanation: Pancreatic lipase digests fats; pancreatic amylase is associated with carbohydrate digestion.

quiz.prompt: Which part of the digestive tract comes immediately after the stomach?
quiz.explanation: The stomach empties via the pylorus into the duodenum, the first section of small intestine.

quiz.prompt: Which statement best distinguishes digestion from absorption?
options: Digestion moves oxygen; absorption removes carbon dioxide
Digestion breaks down food; absorption transfers nutrients into the body
Digestion occurs only in the mouth; absorption only in the stomach
Digestion and absorption mean exactly the same process
quiz.explanation: Digestion prepares absorbable molecules; absorption moves them across intestinal surfaces.

quiz.prompt: If a GI procedure uses oral contrast, what should determine its actual preparation requirements?
options: Current local protocol and clinical orders
A fixed instruction from any old textbook
The result of an unrelated eye test
quiz.explanation: Specific preparation must be checked against the clinical service’s current instructions rather than assuming historical guidance remains valid.

quiz.prompt: Which procedure uses a swallowable camera to obtain GI images?
quiz.explanation: Capsule endoscopy uses a camera capsule to image portions of the gastrointestinal tract.

levels.title: GI tests & common findings
levels.summary: Learn gi tests & common findings through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Purpose of assessment
concepts.body: Gastrointestinal assessment uses the history, physical findings and targeted investigations. The source compares stool tests, abdominal ultrasonography, upper and lower GI contrast studies, endoscopy and capsule endoscopy.
concepts.example: Know what each test visualises, rather than memorising obsolete preparation schedules.

concepts.title: Examples
concepts.body: A stool specimen may be examined for occult blood or organisms. Ultrasonography uses sound waves to visualise abdominal structures. An upper GI contrast study outlines part of the digestive tract using contrast; an endoscopy allows direct mucosal inspection. Capsule endoscopy obtains images as a swallowed camera travels through the tract.
concepts.example: Explain that non-invasive imaging and endoscopy answer different clinical questions.

concepts.title: Nursing focus
concepts.body: Before any investigation, confirm the requested procedure, identity, consent as applicable, allergies, preparation orders and relevant safety checks. Monitor the patient's comfort, symptoms and post-procedure status. Use the institution's CURRENT protocol rather than old timing or medication instructions from the book.
concepts.example: Source is historical: specific fasting, sedation and preparation requirements need current local verification.

quiz.prompt: A stool occult blood test is intended primarily to detect which finding?
quiz.explanation: The source includes stool testing for blood not evident to the naked eye.

quiz.prompt: What type of diagnostic examination directly visualises the inside of the upper GI tract?
quiz.explanation: Endoscopy permits direct observation of the lumen and mucosal surfaces.

quiz.prompt: Which term describes reflux of gastric contents into the oesophagus?
quiz.explanation: Gastro-oesophageal reflux involves backward flow from stomach toward oesophagus.

quiz.prompt: Which anatomical structure is inflamed in appendicitis?
quiz.explanation: Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix.

quiz.prompt: Which finding is classically associated with appendicitis in exam questions?
options: Pain only in the left shoulder
quiz.explanation: The source highlights the right lower quadrant and McBurney’s point in its appendicitis discussion.

levels.title: Appendicitis, peritonitis & obstruction
levels.summary: Learn appendicitis, peritonitis & obstruction through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Peritonitis
concepts.body: The peritoneum is the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering many organs. Peritonitis is inflammation of that membrane; the textbook describes severe abdominal pain, tenderness and guarding as important assessment findings.
concepts.example: Adhesions, hernia and intussusception are pictured in the source.

concepts.title: Intestinal obstruction
concepts.body: Obstruction interferes with the normal onward passage of intestinal contents. The source illustrates adhesions, hernia and intussusception among its causes or mechanisms. Abdominal distention, pain and vomiting can occur, depending on the obstruction.
concepts.example: Melaena refers to dark, tarry stool associated with digested blood.

concepts.title: Hernia
concepts.body: A hernia is protrusion of an organ or tissue through a weakened area. The book distinguishes reducible, irreducible, incarcerated, strangulated and obstructed forms. Suspected strangulation is a medical emergency.
concepts.example: Acute obstruction or peritonitis warrants urgent clinical assessment.

quiz.prompt: What is meant by intestinal obstruction?
options: Impaired onward passage of intestinal contents
quiz.explanation: The source defines intestinal obstruction as interference with normal intestinal transit.

quiz.prompt: Which term refers to inflammation of the peritoneum?
quiz.explanation: Peritonitis is inflammation of the abdominal serous membrane known as the peritoneum.

quiz.prompt: Which condition involves protrusion of tissue through a weakened body wall?
quiz.explanation: A hernia is protrusion of an organ or tissue through a weak region in its surrounding wall.

quiz.prompt: Which is a valid preparation priority before a diagnostic test?
options: Confirm the patient’s identity and order
quiz.explanation: Identity and orders are fundamental preprocedure safety checks; the old textbook’s specific preparation details need current verification.

quiz.prompt: Which postoperative mechanism is a recognised cause of mechanical intestinal obstruction?
quiz.explanation: The source discusses adhesions as an important possible cause of intestinal obstruction, particularly after abdominal surgery.

levels.title: Liver, bile & digestion
levels.summary: Learn liver, bile & digestion through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Liver functions
concepts.body: The liver is a major metabolic organ involved in nutrient processing, protein synthesis, detoxification and bile production. The textbook locates it predominantly in the right upper abdomen and illustrates its relationship to the gallbladder and bile ducts.
concepts.example: Liver produces bile; gallbladder stores and concentrates bile.

concepts.title: Biliary system
concepts.body: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile. Bile travels from the liver through hepatic/biliary ducts and eventually toward the small intestine. Bile helps fat digestion by aiding emulsification.
concepts.example: Bile supports fat digestion but is not itself a digestive enzyme.

concepts.title: Bilirubin
concepts.body: Breakdown of haem produces bilirubin that undergoes hepatic processing and excretion into bile. The source's schematic separates unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin and includes enterohepatic circulation.
concepts.example: The bilirubin pathway helps frame basic jaundice questions.

quiz.prompt: Which organ produces bile?
quiz.explanation: The liver produces bile. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile.

quiz.prompt: Which organ stores and concentrates bile?
quiz.explanation: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder.

quiz.prompt: What is a key digestive function of bile?
options: To break down starch by amylase
quiz.explanation: Bile facilitates fat emulsification, assisting subsequent digestion.

quiz.prompt: Which pancreas-associated enzyme is most connected with carbohydrate digestion?
quiz.explanation: Pancreatic amylase helps digest carbohydrates.

quiz.prompt: Which term means abnormal fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity?
quiz.explanation: Ascites is accumulation of free fluid in the abdominal/peritoneal cavity.

levels.title: Pancreas & biliary conditions
levels.summary: Learn pancreas & biliary conditions through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Pancreas: two functional roles
concepts.body: The pancreas has digestive (exocrine) and hormonal (endocrine) functions. The source lists amylase with carbohydrate digestion, proteolytic enzymes with protein digestion, and lipase with fat digestion.
concepts.example: Amylase → carbohydrate; lipase → fat; proteases → protein.

concepts.title: Gallbladder and bile ducts
concepts.body: Cholelithiasis refers to gallstones; cholecystitis to inflammation of the gallbladder. Their definitions are related but not interchangeable.
concepts.example: Cholelithiasis (stones) differs from cholecystitis (inflammation).

concepts.title: Liver conditions
concepts.body: The source also summarises hepatitis, cirrhosis, portal hypertension and ascites. Ascites is abnormal free-fluid accumulation in the peritoneal cavity. The listed historical nursing interventions need current confirmation before clinical use.
concepts.example: Ascites means free fluid in the peritoneal cavity.

quiz.prompt: What does cholelithiasis mean?
quiz.explanation: Cholelithiasis means stones in the gallbladder or biliary system.

quiz.prompt: Into which section of the small intestine does bile ultimately flow?
quiz.explanation: Bile drains through the biliary system into the duodenum, the first segment of the small intestine.

quiz.prompt: Which condition denotes inflammation of pancreatic tissue?
quiz.explanation: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas.

quiz.prompt: Which option is the safest interpretation of an older nursing textbook?
options: Historic management plans must be checked against current evidence
The textbook should replace hospital policies
quiz.explanation: Clinical guidance evolves; older printed guidance can be used for exam context but must be verified before real-world application.

quiz.prompt: Which term means inflammation of the gallbladder?
quiz.explanation: Cholecystitis describes gallbladder inflammation; cholelithiasis describes gallstones.

levels.title: Ear structure & balance
levels.summary: Learn ear structure & balance through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Three anatomical regions
concepts.body: The external ear includes the auricle and external auditory canal and directs sound inward. The tympanic membrane separates the external canal from the middle-ear cavity.
concepts.example: Ossicles: malleus, incus and stapes.

concepts.title: Middle ear
concepts.body: The ossicles are malleus, incus and stapes. They transmit vibrations from the tympanic membrane toward the inner ear. The auditory (Eustachian) tube connects the middle ear to the nasopharynx and helps equalise pressure.
concepts.example: Cochlea is linked to hearing; semicircular canals are linked to balance.

concepts.title: Inner ear
concepts.body: The cochlea is important for hearing. Vestibular structures, including semicircular canals, participate in balance. The vestibulocochlear nerve carries hearing and balance information toward the brain.
concepts.example: A perforated tympanic membrane may affect sound conduction.

quiz.prompt: Which trio forms the middle-ear ossicles?
quiz.explanation: The ossicles are malleus, incus and stapes.

quiz.prompt: Which structure separates the external auditory canal from the middle-ear cavity?
quiz.explanation: The eardrum (tympanic membrane) marks the boundary between external canal and middle ear.

quiz.prompt: Which inner-ear structure is chiefly associated with hearing?
quiz.explanation: The cochlea contains sensory structures for hearing.

quiz.prompt: Which inner-ear structures contribute prominently to balance?
quiz.explanation: Semicircular canals form part of the vestibular balance apparatus.

quiz.prompt: Which bedside test compares air and bone conduction?
quiz.explanation: The Rinne tuning-fork test compares sound perceived through air and bone conduction.

levels.title: Hearing assessment & ENT conditions
levels.summary: Learn hearing assessment & ent conditions through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Hearing assessment
concepts.body: The textbook describes tuning-fork tests and audiometry. They test different aspects of hearing and must be interpreted alongside history and examination.
concepts.example: Rinne compares air and bone conduction.

concepts.title: Rinne test
concepts.body: A vibrating tuning fork is used to compare air conduction and bone conduction at one ear. In a typical normal hearing pattern, air conduction lasts longer than bone conduction.
concepts.example: Weber assesses sound lateralisation.

concepts.title: Weber test
concepts.body: A vibrating tuning fork is positioned at the midline of the skull. The examiner asks whether sound is perceived equally or more loudly on one side; lateralisation provides an important clue.
concepts.example: Audiometry plots hearing thresholds; it is not the same as otoscopy.

quiz.prompt: Which bedside hearing test examines sound lateralisation?
quiz.explanation: Weber assessment uses a midline tuning fork to assess sound lateralisation.

quiz.prompt: Which anatomical portion of the ear houses the cochlea?
quiz.explanation: The cochlea is within the inner ear.

quiz.prompt: What does epistaxis mean?
quiz.explanation: Epistaxis is the clinical term for bleeding from the nose.

quiz.prompt: Which examination directly investigates ear canal and tympanic membrane appearance?
quiz.explanation: Otoscopy allows examination of the external canal and eardrum.

quiz.prompt: Which paired test names both relate to hearing assessment?
quiz.explanation: Rinne and Weber are bedside tuning-fork hearing tests.

levels.title: Eye anatomy & visual assessment
levels.summary: Learn eye anatomy & visual assessment through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Three coats of the eyeball
concepts.body: The textbook illustrates a fibrous outer layer (including sclera and cornea), vascular middle layer (including choroid) and sensory inner layer (retina).
concepts.example: Cornea and lens refract light.

concepts.title: Lens and pupil
concepts.body: The lens helps focus light. The iris controls pupil diameter. The cornea provides much of the eye's refraction, while the retina contains photoreceptors that convert light into neural signals.
concepts.example: Retina houses photoreceptors; optic nerve carries visual signals.

concepts.title: Important landmarks
concepts.body: The macula is an area of detailed central vision; the optic disc is where the optic nerve exits the eye and normally has no photoreceptors. The optic nerve transmits visual information to the brain.
concepts.example: The optic disc is the normal physiological blind spot.

quiz.prompt: Which ocular structure contains photoreceptor cells?
quiz.explanation: The retina contains rods and cones involved in visual phototransduction.

quiz.prompt: What is the main role of the lens?
options: To focus light toward the retina
quiz.explanation: The crystalline lens helps focus incoming light onto the retina.

quiz.prompt: Which chart is commonly used to assess visual acuity?
quiz.explanation: The textbook describes the Snellen chart for measuring visual acuity.

quiz.prompt: What does tonometry measure?
quiz.explanation: Tonometry measures intraocular pressure, an important part of glaucoma assessment.

quiz.prompt: Which condition is caused by opacity of the crystalline lens?
quiz.explanation: Cataract is opacity/clouding of the crystalline lens.

levels.title: Visual disorders & nursing priorities
levels.summary: Learn visual disorders & nursing priorities through three structured lessons and five source-linked exam-style questions. All questions are newly adapted study practice, not original numbered textbook MCQs.
objectives: Explain the core concepts and anatomical relationships.
Apply distinctions in five four-option practice questions.

concepts.title: Assessment tests
concepts.body: The textbook describes visual acuity using a Snellen chart, colour vision testing and tonometry. Visual acuity estimates resolving ability, while tonometry measures intraocular pressure.
concepts.example: Snellen chart → visual acuity; tonometry → intraocular pressure.

concepts.title: Refractive errors
concepts.body: Myopia (nearsightedness) causes difficulty seeing distant objects; hyperopia commonly affects near focusing. Astigmatism involves unequal curvature of optical surfaces, causing blurred/distorted images.
concepts.example: Myopia → trouble focusing on distant objects.

concepts.title: Cataract and retinal conditions
concepts.body: Cataract is opacity of the crystalline lens. Retinal detachment is separation of neural retina from supporting tissue and may threaten vision. Sudden visual loss warrants urgent evaluation.
concepts.example: Cataract involves lens opacity; glaucoma is an optic neuropathy.

quiz.prompt: Myopia is most directly associated with difficulty seeing what?
quiz.explanation: Myopia is nearsightedness, often producing blurred distance vision.

quiz.prompt: Which nerve conveys signals from the retina toward the brain?
quiz.explanation: The optic nerve carries visual signals toward the brain.

quiz.prompt: Which eye structure adjusts the amount of incoming light by controlling pupil size?
quiz.explanation: The iris changes the pupil diameter to regulate light entry.

quiz.prompt: A patient reporting sudden loss of vision needs which action?
quiz.explanation: Acute visual loss can signal an urgent eye condition and should be assessed promptly.

quiz.prompt: Which method specifically evaluates the eye’s internal pressure?
quiz.explanation: Tonometry is an ophthalmic investigation used to assess intraocular pressure.
